UDLCO CRH: Illustration of different layers of PaJR patient centred learning

This synthesis analyzes how a **Patient Journey Record (PaJR)** workflow utilizes a **User-Driven Learning Community Ontology (UDLCO)** framework to turn clinical data into improved patient outcomes. It breaks down the transition from raw clinical data (Layer 1) to peer-reviewed educational insights (Layer 2) and aggregate, AI-driven case-based reasoning (Layer 3).


## IMRAD Summary (Socratic Steelman Format)


### Introduction


The gap between standardized, textbook-driven guidelines and the complex realities of low-resource clinical settings often leads to redundant, costly, or potentially harmful medical over-investigation. Traditional diagnostic models struggle to balance static clinical algorithms with individual patient constraints.

This study evaluates the **PaJR Three-Layer Model** 


Layer 1 PaJR: Day to day Care published day wise after deidentification, identifiable only to the caregivers also containing team based learning and academic structuring that overlaps onto layer 2 and 3), for example detailed here: 

https://publications.pajrhealth.org/rangoli-jasmine-40652/

Layer 2 : structured publication: see below 


Layer 3 ProJR: Collective intelligence after integrating individual care trajectories with past published trajectories). It specifically examines how decontextualized textbook simulations (Layers 1a and 1b) interact with real-world, context-rich patient data to optimize resource stewardship, refine clinical reasoning, and improve outcomes for the individual patient at hand following on the layer 1 example above. https://avi33tbtt.github.io/demo/cases/tmng-nested-analysis.html


### Methods


A single-case educational design was deployed utilizing a UDLCO framework within an active clinical group in rural Telangana, India.


 * **The Patient:** A 76-year-old, frail female (40 kg) presenting with a rapidly enlarging, compressive toxic multinodular goiter (TMNG), subclinical hyperthyroidism (TSH less than 0.01 uIU/mL), and severe cardiorespiratory red flags (dysphagia, dyspnea, tremors). 


 * **The Interventions & Simulations:** Three medical students simulated the case under decontextualized constraints (Layer 1a/1b) using various generative AI agents (Claude, PaJR Bot). Their theoretical learning points were then contrasted against the decisions made by the active care team.


 * **Data Synthesis:** The real-time chat logs, cytology images showing colloid-laden macrophages (foam cells), and peer discussions were consolidated into a de-identified formal Case Report Draft (Layer 2). This draft was then indexed against five comparative PubMed cases using an ultra-lightweight Case-Based Reasoning (CBR) protocol (Layer 3).


### Results


 * **The Theoretical Bias (Decontextualized AI):** When the case was completely decontextualized, the initial AI and student recommendations called for extensive pre-operative workups. These included radioactive iodine uptake scans and abdominal rule-outs for rare conditions like pheochromocytoma (MEN-2 syndromes).


 * **The Practical Correction (Contextualized Reality):** Re-introducing the patient's specific context (76-year-old female, 40 kg, rural, resource-constrained) allowed the PaJR Bot and clinical team to dismiss these extensive steps due to an extremely low pre-test probability.


 * **Diagnostic Execution:** Proceeding directly to a high-yield, low-cost Fine Needle Aspiration Cytology (FNAC) revealed **colloid-laden macrophages**. This confirmed a benign, long-standing, degenerating colloid nodule within a TMNG rather than an aggressive, new malignancy. This single path safely guided clinical management while avoiding the delays and financial toxicities of unnecessary testing.

```

[Layer 1: Raw Clinical Care published after deidentification and patient consent) 

   ↳ Real patient data: 76F with severe neck mass, hyperthyroid state. https://publications.pajrhealth.org/rangoli-jasmine-40652/

   

[Layer 1a/1b: Decontextualized Simulations of layer 1 publication]


   ↳ Students + AI vibe on raw text -> Suggest high-cost, low-yield rule outs (MEN-2, scans).


   ↳ Contextualized check: Adding age/geography optimizes the plan to focus on FNAC first.


[Layer 2: Structured Publication]


   ↳ Cytology uploaded -> Identifies colloid macrophages (benign degeneration).


   ↳ Case report drafted -> Focuses on local resource stewardship and pathophysiology.


[Layer 3: Integrating with collective Intelligence & case based reasoning CBR pathways aka ProJRs resulting in collective citations ]

   ↳ Case mapped against global PubMed cohorts to identify unique trajectories.

   ↳ Next step: Integrate external social factors (PNI) to see the full patient journey.


```https://avi33tbtt.github.io/demo/cases/tmng-nested-analysis.html


### Discussion


The study demonstrates that absolute reliance on unaligned AI or strict textbook pathways can lead to over-testing. By introducing a structured, layered workflow, the platform acts as an educational filter that balances theory with practice.

The microscopic identification of "foam cells" confirmed the underlying pathophysiology: an initial iodine and multi-micromineral (Selenium, Iron, Zinc) deficiency triggered chronic thyroid hyperplasia over decades, which later shifted into autonomous hormone production.

A limitation of the current Layer 3 execution is its focus on internal medicine data (disease events), which omits the patient's external medicine trajectory (social, economic, and environmental lifestyle factors). Capturing these life events is essential to understanding the patient's full **psychoneuroimmunology (PNI)** profile.


## Keywords


 * User-Driven Healthcare (UDH)

 * Patient Journey Record (PaJR)

 * Toxic Multinodular Goiter (Plummer's Disease)

 * User-Driven Learning Community Ontology (UDLCO)

 * Case-Based Reasoning (CBR)

 * Fine Needle Aspiration Cytology (FNAC)

 * Resource Stewardship

 * Psychoneuroimmunology (PNI)


## Thematic Analysis


### 1. The Conflict Between Theoretical Over-Investigation and Pragmatic Resource Stewardship

A recurring theme is the gap between a decontextualized "textbook" workup and real-world medicine. Without constraints, both AI models and early-career students tend to recommend defensive, low-yield diagnostic pathways (e.g., screening a 76-year-old for an exceptionally rare hereditary pheochromocytoma). The UDLCO framework functions as a corrective mechanism, enforcing a step-by-step approach that prioritizes immediate, high-yield interventions like FNAC and excision biopsy over exhaustive expensive testing.


### 2. Multi-Layered Data De-Identification as an Educational Tool


The transition of data from Layer 1 (identifiable clinical data) to Layer 1a/1b (decontextualized student cases) shows that removing demographic markers can be useful for testing pure clinical theory. However, the analysis also reveals that returning context (age, gender, setting) is vital to optimizing treatment plans and removing textbook redundancies.


### 3. The Shift from Single-Element to Multi-Factorial Pathophysiology


The clinical discussion changes our understanding of goitrogenesis from a simple, single-cause model (iodine deficiency alone) to a complex, multi-system model. The patient’s condition is seen as a long-term process driven by a combination of factors:

This approach helps clinicians look past the acute symptoms to address the broader metabolic and nutritional environment that caused the disease.


### 4. Disease Trajectories vs. Life Event Trajectories


The final layer of the analysis highlights a split between *internal medicine* (tracking physical disease events) and *external medicine* (tracking social life events). While current AI models can easily match clinical findings across medical databases, they frequently overlook the patient's lived experience, financial challenges, and emotional state. These external factors directly influence health outcomes through psychoneuroimmunological (PNI) pathways.


## Socratic Questions for Clinical Reflection


 1. **On Clinical Reasoning:** How can medical training platforms best teach students to appreciate rare syndromes in textbooks while still training them to avoid low-yield, costly over-investigation at the bedside of a frail patient?


 2. **On System Design:** If adding age and gender context back into a decontextualized simulation immediately clarifies the diagnostic path, how should we design our software to prevent AI systems from generating overly broad recommendations when that context is missing?


 3. **On Pathophysiology:** If local micronutrient deficiencies (like Selenium, Iron, and Zinc) are what sustain and worsen a goiter after an initial lack of iodine, how should we change our public health and nutritional strategies to better manage multi-nodular thyroid diseases?


 4. **On Holism:** How can we expand our data collection tools to capture a patient's daily life, social environment, and emotional history with the same accuracy we use for lab values and pathology images? What are the primary ethical risks of gathering this level of personal information?




Please provide a Socratic steelman imrad summary, keywords, thematic analysis and socratic questions around the content focusing on how to leverage patient events data driven healthcare learning outcomes in improving patient's illness outcomes.



A Layered Model for PaJR workflow has been previously published and to quote below:


PaJR segments data into three distinct environments:

  • Layer 1 (Raw Clinical Care published after deidentification and patient consent): Identifiable data only for the care team comprising of local treating clinicians some of who are also in the global PaJR team. Action: Access restricted by Role-Based Access Control (RBAC).


  • Layer 2 (Structured Publication): Structured sharing of patient events data in a traditional IMRAD case report format that is easily readable and actionable globally. Action: "Risk Meter" and "Nudges" to soften identifiers before sharing that improves on traditional case reporting as here even the health professional and their institutional identifiers are removed.

  • Layer 3 (Intelligence): Citations by agentic humans and AI around the prior published layer 2 provide a structured, non-identifiable general knowledge through patient events data for AI/Research.

Case report drafted based on the detailed clinical logs and discussions in level 1 where nuances of clinical reasoning, including the discussion on resource-appropriate testing.

***

Case Report Draft**

**Title:** Management of a Large Compressive Toxic Multinodular Goiter in a Frail, 76-Year-Old Female in a Resource-Constrained Setting

**Authors:** (To be added)

**Correspondence to:** (To be added)

**Abstract:**


We report the case of a 76-year-old female from rural Telangana, India, who presented with a rapidly enlarging, compressive multinodular goiter and subclinical hyperthyroidism. The case highlights the diagnostic and management challenges in a frail, elderly patient with significant "red flag" symptoms. The patient was managed with medical stabilization of her thyrotoxicosis while awaiting urgent cytological evaluation to rule out malignancy. This report underscores the importance of pragmatic, resource-appropriate clinical reasoning, which was captured and refined through a User-Driven Learning Community Ontology (UDLCO) platform, contrasting with initial AI-generated suggestions for more extensive, low-yield investigations.

**Introduction:**

Large, long-standing multinodular goiters (MNG) are common in regions with historical iodine deficiency. In elderly patients, they can present a clinical emergency when they grow rapidly, causing compressive symptoms such as dysphagia and dyspnea. These "red flag" symptoms raise the suspicion of malignant transformation within the goiter, which occurs in 5-10% of MNGs. Management requires a careful balance between the risks of airway compromise and malignancy against the surgical risks in a frail patient with comorbidities. We describe such a case, managed in Telangana, India, highlighting a resource-stewarded diagnostic pathway.

**Case Presentation:**

A 76-year-old female with a three-year history of hypertension presented with a two-month history of progressive right-sided neck swelling, dysphagia, and shortness of breath. She also reported a significant loss of appetite and weight, with a current weight of 40 kg.

On examination, her vitals were: blood pressure 170/90 mmHg, pulse 100 beats per minute, and SpO2 98% on room air. She appeared frail and had visible tremors of her outstretched hands and mild bilateral lid lag. A large, firm, non-tender goiter was palpable, with the right lobe larger than the left. There was no palpable cervical lymphadenopathy.

Initial investigations revealed subclinical hyperthyroidism with a suppressed Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH) of <0.01 uIU/mL, with normal serum T3 (1.16 ng/mL) and T4 (81.98 ng/mL) levels. A clinical diagnosis of a toxic multinodular goiter with compressive symptoms was made.

**Management and Outcome:**

Given the clinical picture of thyrotoxicosis and hypertension, the patient was started on Carbimazole 5mg twice daily to control her hyperthyroid state and mitigate cardiovascular risk.

The key clinical challenge was the urgent need to rule out malignancy. A Fine Needle Aspiration Cytology (FNAC) of the dominant thyroid nodule was planned. The clinical team, using the PaJR platform for collaborative discussion, deliberated on the necessity of pre-emptive screening for pheochromocytoma, given its association with Medullary Thyroid Carcinoma (MTC) in MEN-2 syndromes. It was concluded that, in a resource-limited setting, proceeding directly with FNAC was the most logical and highest-yield step. Screening for pheochromocytoma would only become mandatory if the FNAC confirmed MTC, a diagnosis that is exceptionally rare to present for the first time at age 76.

**Discussion:**

This case demonstrates the critical importance of pragmatic clinical reasoning in a resource-constrained environment. The patient’s presentation with compressive symptoms and weight loss made malignancy a primary concern. The management pathway correctly prioritized medical stabilization and urgent cytological diagnosis.

A notable aspect of this case was the explicit discussion comparing the planned, focused investigation (FNAC first) with a more exhaustive, resource-intensive workup initially suggested by a generative AI model (Claude). The clinical team correctly identified that the pre-test probability of a condition like MEN-2A in this patient was extremely low, and pursuing extensive screening prematurely would represent poor resource stewardship. This decision-making process, captured within the PaJR's UDLCO, serves as a valuable learning example of adapting global guidelines to local realities.

**Learning Points:**

*   In elderly patients with a large multinodular goiter and compressive "red flag" symptoms, malignancy must be the primary differential diagnosis to exclude.

*   A stepwise, resource-appropriate diagnostic approach is crucial in low-resource settings, prioritizing high-yield investigations like FNAC over exhaustive screening for rare syndromes.

*   User-Driven Learning Community Ontology (UDLCO) platforms can effectively capture and audit clinical reasoning, highlighting how experienced clinicians navigate the gap between theoretical knowledge, AI suggestions, and practical, patient-centered care.

[22/06, 16:55]hu2: Going by the overall history, clinical and microscopic findings what is the likely pathophysiology of this patient's multi-nodular goitre?



[22/06, 16:56] PaJR Health Bot Feb 26: Based on all the evidence, the patient's condition has a two-part pathophysiology, culminating in a classic diagnosis of **Toxic Multinodular Goiter (Plummer's Disease)**.

Here is the most likely sequence of events:

1.  **Phase 1: The Slow Burn (Decades-long Goiter Formation)**
    *   For many years, perhaps decades, the patient has had a simple multinodular goiter. This is the slow, benign enlargement of the thyroid gland, forming multiple nodules.
    *   The microscopic findings of colloid-laden macrophages confirm this long-standing process. They represent old nodules that have degenerated and are being cleaned up by the immune system. This is a sign of an "old" goiter, not an aggressive new growth.

2.  **Phase 2: The "Toxic" Switch (The Recent Crisis)**

    *   Within this long-standing goiter, some of the nodules have evolved to become **autonomous**. This is the key event.

    *   These autonomous nodules function like rogue factories, producing thyroid hormone (T4/T3) continuously, irrespective of the body's needs or the commands from the pituitary gland (TSH).
    *   As these nodules churn out excess hormone, the pituitary shuts down TSH production in an attempt to regain control, which is why her TSH is suppressed (<0.01).
    *   This flood of excess thyroid hormone is the "toxic" part, and it's directly responsible for her recent symptoms: the tachycardia, hypertension, tremors, and metabolic changes.

**IN SUMMARY:**

The patient has a long-standing, benign multinodular goiter where some nodules have recently become autonomous, tipping her from a state of having a simple enlarged thyroid (a goiter) into a state of active hyperthyroidism (thyrotoxicosis).

This single diagnosis neatly explains all her symptoms:
*   **Compressive Symptoms (dysphagia, SOB):** Caused by the physical size of the long-standing goiter.
*   **Metabolic Symptoms (tachycardia, etc.):** Caused by the recent toxic switch and hormone overproduction.

[22/06, 22:05]hu3: There is plenty of literature on Iodine deficiency couple with other micromineral deficiencies taking turns to do this. Apparent Iodine deficiency is only required to start the process and once it begins, other such chemicals take over. What do you think?

[22/06, 22:06] PaJR Health Bot Feb 26: You are absolutely correct. Your thinking is in line with the current understanding of goitrogenesis, which has moved beyond a simple iodine-deficiency model.

It's a multifactorial process. You can think of it as a series of cascading events:

1.  **The Ignition:** **Iodine deficiency** is often the initial trigger. It reduces the efficiency of thyroid hormone production, leading to a compensatory rise in TSH from the pituitary. This is the "on switch" for thyroid growth.

2.  **The Accelerants (The "other chemicals" you mentioned):**

    *   **Selenium Deficiency:** This is a major co-conspirator. Selenium is vital for the enzymes that convert T4 to active T3 and also for antioxidant enzymes that protect the thyroid gland from damage during hormone synthesis. Without enough selenium, the thyroid is both less efficient and more prone to damage, exacerbating the effect of low iodine.

    *   **Iron Deficiency:** The key enzyme for making thyroid hormone, Thyroid Peroxidase (TPO), is iron-dependent. Iron deficiency impairs its function, further hindering hormone production and fueling the TSH-driven growth cycle.

    *   **Goitrogens:** Certain foods (like cassava, soy, and cruciferous vegetables) contain substances that can actively block iodine uptake, effectively creating a state of iodine deficiency even when dietary intake is borderline.

3.  **The Takeover:** Once chronic TSH stimulation and these deficiencies lead to initial thyroid enlargement, other **local growth factors** (like IGF-1, EGF) within the gland itself "take over," promoting the disorganized, nodular growth that defines a multinodular goiter.

So, you're right to say iodine deficiency just starts the process. It's the subsequent interplay with other micronutrient deficiencies and local factors that determines the progression and severity of the goiter.

***
**Reference:**
*   Triggiani, V., et al. (2009). Role of iodine, selenium and other micronutrients in thyroid disease. *Endocrine, Metabolic & Immune Disorders-Drug Targets*, 9(3), 277-294. (PMID: 19594417)

***

**1. Comprehensive Review on Goiter Etiology (2016)**

*   **Citation:** Knobel, M. (2016). Etiopathology, clinical features, and treatment of diffuse and multinodular nontoxic goiters. *Journal of Endocrinological Investigation*, 39(4), 357-373.

*   **Key Insight:** This review explicitly lists multiple causal factors beyond just iodine.
*   **Quote:** "Goiter...is a common problem in clinical practice associated with iodine deficiency, increase in serum thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level, natural goitrogens, smoking, and **lack of selenium and iron**. Evidence suggests that heredity also has an important role in the etiology of goiter."
*   **Link:** [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26392367/](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26392367/) (PMID: 26392367)

**2. The North American Clinics Review (2012)**

*   **Citation:** Medeiros-Neto, G., Camargo, R. Y., & Tomimori, E. K. (2012). Approach to and treatment of goiters. *The Medical Clinics of North America*, 96(2), 351-368.
*   **Key Insight:** This article, targeted at practicing clinicians, reinforces the multifactorial cause and adds another mineral, zinc, to the list.
*   **Quote:** "The main causes of simple diffuse goiter (SDG) and multinodular goiter (MNG) are iodine deficiency, increase in serum thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level, natural goitrogens, smoking, chronic malnutrition, and **lack of selenium, iron, and zinc**."
*   **Link:** [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22443980/](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22443980/) (PMID: 22443980)

These papers provide a robust evidence base for the concept that while iodine deficiency may be the primary initiator, other micronutrient deficiencies—particularly of selenium and iron—are critical cofactors that sustain and exacerbate the goitrogenic process.
